title: Yields Ease, Jobs Cool, Micron Surges
summary: This week’s quick briefing covers record US equity highs, easing bond yields, softer US jobs data and lower oil prices. We also unpack Micron’s extraordinary AI-memory results, Nike’s early-stage turnaround, and the key UK-time events to watch next week.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: US shares hit fresh highs, but the bigger story is the tug-of-war between falling yields, weaker jobs, cheaper oil and very expensive AI optimism.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Welcome to The Weekly Market Brief, covering Tuesday the twenty-ninth of September to Tuesday the sixth of October twenty twenty-six. As ever, this is general information, not personal financial advice, so please do your own research.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: First story: bond yields — basically the interest rate governments pay to borrow — eased late in the week, and that helped the S&P 500 and Nasdaq reach records on Tuesday.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right, but the warning light hasn’t gone out. Earlier in the week, global government bond yields were reported near multi-decade highs, and the Bank of England flagged elevated risk in gilt markets.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And gilts are UK government bonds, for anyone not living inside a rates terminal.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. The Bank said adjustments had mostly been gradual so far, but hedge-fund borrowing in the gilt market remained elevated. Dry phrase, real risk.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So what does this mean for a normal investor?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Lower yields can help growth shares and technology valuations. But if long-term yields jump again, that’s a headwind for bond funds, expensive equities, and mortgage-sensitive parts of the market.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second story: the US labour market cooled sharply. September payrolls rose by just twenty-nine thousand, and unemployment was four point two percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That supports the idea that the US central bank may not need to raise rates in October. But the obvious question is: good news, or bad news?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Because weaker jobs can mean lower rate pressure, but also weaker demand.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. It helps rate-sensitive shares only if it doesn’t turn into an earnings problem. So this is not simply “bad jobs equals good markets”.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Third story: oil. OPEC said seven countries would keep November production at September-required levels, while reports of higher Middle East exports and planned G7 stock releases pushed oil lower.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That matters because cheaper oil can help airlines, logistics companies, households and inflation expectations. But conflict risk hasn’t disappeared, so energy prices remain a live risk.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, earnings worth knowing. First, Micron. This was the stand-out AI-related result of the week.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Stand-out is doing some work there. Micron reported about fifty-four billion dollars of revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter, up from about eleven billion a year earlier. Official net income was about thirty-eight billion dollars.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And management guided the next quarter’s revenue to around sixty-two billion dollars, give or take.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which says AI infrastructure demand is feeding through to memory pricing and margins. But memory chips are historically cyclical. Exceptional margins can reverse quickly if supply catches up or customers slow spending.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second earnings story: Nike. Revenue was eleven point two billion dollars, down four percent, but gross margin improved by about half a percentage point.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That’s the turnaround tension in one sentence. Costs and margins are improving, but revenue is still falling, and the company expects fiscal-year revenue to decline by high single digits.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So this isn’t yet a clean growth story.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: No. It’s a restructuring story trying to become a product momentum story. The risk is that savings get the attention, while China, digital sales and brand heat still need to stabilise.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Quick week ahead. Wednesday at seven p.m. UK time, the Fed minutes land, from the September meeting.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Markets will look for how seriously policymakers discussed inflation and oil risks versus softer jobs data. That mix matters for bonds, currencies and growth shares.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Thursday brings PepsiCo: release at eleven a.m., analyst questions at one fifteen p.m. UK time. Tesco also reports interims, with UK grocery volumes and price investment in focus.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then Friday at three p.m., Delta Air Lines has its September-quarter webcast, with read-throughs for oil, premium travel and corporate demand.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Quick recap: yields eased but bond-market risk remains; softer US jobs lower rate pressure but raise growth questions; and oil relief helps, but isn’t guaranteed.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And on earnings, Micron’s numbers were extraordinary, with cyclical risks attached, while Nike’s turnaround is still early and messy.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That’s The Weekly Market Brief. Links are in the show notes. Final reminder: this is general information, not personal financial advice. Do your own research, and we’ll be back next week.
